We propose a time-varying Poisson autoregression (TVPAR) model that extends the standard Poisson autoregression (PAR) model by incorporating time-varying parameters. The TVPAR model is based on a Poisson distribution with a time-varying mean that is modeled using a linear combination of lagged values of the response variable and time-varying coefficients. We use a Bayesian approach to estimate the TVPAR model, where the time-varying coefficients are modeled using a random walk prior. We also propose a Bayesian information criterion (BIC) for model selection and a likelihood ratio test for testing the significance of the time-varying coefficients. We apply the TVPAR model to a real-world dataset of daily crime counts in Chicago and compare its performance with the standard PAR model. The results show that the TVPAR model provides a better fit to the data and captures the time-varying patterns in the crime counts more accurately than the standard PAR model.

Stellar photometry has been used to measure aerosol optical depth (AOD) in the past, but recent advancements have improved its accuracy and applicability. This paper discusses the new developments in aerosol measurements using stellar photometry, including the use of machine learning algorithms to improve the accuracy of AOD retrievals and the extension of the method to measure aerosol properties such as single-scattering albedo and aerosol size distribution. The paper also discusses the potential of stellar photometry to measure aerosol properties in regions with limited ground-based measurements, such as remote or polar regions.

We present a novel method for configurational molecular sampling that combines the efficiency of Langevin dynamics with the robustness of a recently introduced adaptive thermostat. Our approach, which we call adaptive Langevin dynamics, is designed to efficiently sample the configurational space of complex molecular systems while maintaining robustness against temperature fluctuations. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method by applying it to a variety of molecular systems, including a Lennard-Jones fluid, a polyatomic molecule, and a protein. Our results show that adaptive Langevin dynamics outperforms traditional Langevin dynamics in terms of sampling efficiency and robustness, and is comparable to or even surpasses the performance of more advanced sampling methods. We also provide a detailed analysis of the adaptive thermostat and its role in maintaining robustness, as well as a discussion of the implications of our results for the development of efficient and robust molecular simulation methods.

This paper presents a comprehensive evaluation of the use of human reference data for assessing the quality of automatic image descriptions. The authors investigate the impact of reference data quality, diversity, and quantity on the evaluation of image description models. They also examine the effect of reference data on the evaluation of different aspects of image description, including content, coherence, and fluency. The results of the study suggest that high-quality reference data is essential for accurate evaluation, and that the use of diverse and large-scale reference data can lead to more reliable and generalizable results. The authors also propose a new evaluation framework that takes into account the limitations of reference data and provides a more comprehensive assessment of image description models.

We derive a new expression for the complexity of conformal field theories (CFTs) using the Euler-Arnold equations. The Euler-Arnold equations describe the geodesic motion of a curve on a Lie group, and we use them to construct a new action functional that encodes the complexity of a CFT. We show that this action functional is related to the complexity of a CFT, and we use it to derive a new expression for the complexity of a CFT in terms of the Euler-Arnold equations. We also discuss the implications of our results for the study of CFTs and the holographic principle.

We present a comprehensive analysis of the predictions of additional baryons and mesons based on the quark model. We use the mass formula of the quark model to predict the masses of the additional baryons and mesons. We also use the mass formula to predict the masses of the additional baryons and mesons that are not yet observed. We find that the mass formula is able to predict the masses of the additional baryons and mesons with a high degree of accuracy. We also find that the mass formula is able to predict the masses of the additional baryons and mesons that are not yet observed with a high degree of accuracy.

In this paper, we explore the concept of wideband waveforming for integrated data and energy transfer. We introduce the SISO-OFDM and MISO-OFDM counterparts to the wideband waveforming technique, which was previously proposed for multiple antennas and multiple carriers. The SISO-OFDM counterpart is a single-antenna, single-carrier system that achieves the same level of performance as the original wideband waveforming technique. The MISO-OFDM counterpart is a multiple-antenna, multiple-carrier system that achieves even better performance than the original technique. We provide a detailed analysis of the SISO-OFDM and MISO-OFDM counterparts, including their system models, signal processing techniques, and performance metrics. We also provide numerical results to demonstrate the effectiveness of the SISO-OFDM and MISO-OFDM counterparts in various scenarios.

We present a theory pipeline for fitting the proton structure function F2(x,Q^2) to experimental data. The pipeline is based on the DGLAP evolution equations and the BFKL equation, which describe the evolution of the parton distribution functions (PDFs) with Q^2. We use the DGLAP evolution equations to evolve the PDFs from a low Q^2 reference point to the experimental Q^2, and then use the BFKL equation to evolve the PDFs from the reference point to a higher Q^2. We use the experimental data to constrain the PDFs at the reference point, and then use the evolved PDFs to make predictions for the structure function F2(x,Q^2) at the experimental Q^2. We compare our results to the experimental data and find good agreement. We also compare our results to the results of other PDF fitting groups and find that our results are consistent with theirs.

A linearized framework is developed to model the response of a turbulent jet flame to acoustic forcing. The active flame approach is used to describe the flame dynamics, where the flame is treated as an active medium that interacts with the acoustic field. The framework is based on the Navier-Stokes equations and the flame is modelled using a level-set method. The acoustic field is described using a linearized Euler equation. The interaction between the flame and the acoustic field is modelled using a forcing term in the flame equation of state. The response of the flame to acoustic forcing is studied using a harmonic forcing function. The results show that the flame response is strongly dependent on the frequency of the forcing function and the amplitude of the acoustic field. The framework is validated against experimental data and is shown to be in good agreement. The results of this study have implications for the design of combustion systems that are resistant to acoustic forcing.

We present a nonlocal gravity theory based on the fundamental tetrad field, which is a nonlocal generalization of the Einstein-Cartan theory. The fundamental tetrad field is a nonlocal function of the metric field, and it satisfies a nonlocal equation of motion. We derive the constitutive relations for the fundamental tetrad field, which describe the relationship between the fundamental tetrad field and the metric field. We also derive the nonlocal equation of motion for the fundamental tetrad field, which is a nonlocal generalization of the Einstein field equation. We show that the nonlocal gravity theory based on the fundamental tetrad field is a nonlocal generalization of the Einstein-Cartan theory, and it reduces to the Einstein-Cartan theory in the local limit. We also discuss the implications of the nonlocal gravity theory based on the fundamental tetrad field for the behavior of gravitational waves and the properties of black holes.

The Large Hadron Collider (LHC) is a powerful tool for studying the properties of matter at the smallest scales. The LHC is a circular tunnel that is 27 kilometers in circumference and is located at CERN, the European Organization for Nuclear Research. The LHC is used to accelerate protons to nearly the speed of light and then collide them at four points around the ring. The collisions produce a wide range of subatomic particles, which are then detected and analyzed by sophisticated detectors. The LHC has made several groundbreaking discoveries, including the detection of the Higgs boson, which is a fundamental particle that is responsible for giving other particles mass. The LHC has also made significant contributions to our understanding of the strong nuclear force, which holds quarks together inside protons and neutrons. In addition, the LHC has been used to study the properties of quarks and gluons, which are the building blocks of protons and neutrons. The LHC has also been used to search for new physics beyond the Standard Model, which is the current theory of particle physics. The LHC has the potential to make many more groundbreaking discoveries in the future, and it will continue to be a major tool for advancing our understanding of the universe.

We present a comprehensive analysis of the recurrence times of neutron star X-ray binary transients and the nature of the Galactic Centre quiescent X-ray binaries. Our study is based on a sample of 24 transient neutron star low-mass X-ray binaries (LMXBs) and 14 quiescent LMXBs in the Galactic Centre. We find that the recurrence times of transient LMXBs are strongly correlated with their orbital periods, with longer orbital periods corresponding to longer recurrence times. This correlation is consistent with the idea that the recurrence times are determined by the orbital period of the binary system. We also find that the quiescent LMXBs in the Galactic Centre have longer recurrence times than the transient LMXBs, suggesting that they may be in a different state of activity. Our results have implications for our understanding of the accretion process in neutron star LMXBs and the nature of the Galactic Centre quiescent X-ray binaries.

We present an FPT algorithm for the Bipartite Vertex Splitting problem, which is a generalization of the well-known Vertex Cover problem. Given a bipartite graph G = (U, V, E) and a positive integer k, the problem asks whether there exists a partition of the vertices of G into two sets U' and V' such that |U'| = k and the subgraph induced by U' has at most one edge incident to each vertex in V'. We show that the problem can be solved in O(2^k \cdot n^2) time, where n is the number of vertices in G. This result is obtained by a reduction to the problem of finding a minimum vertex cover in a bipartite graph, which can be solved in O(2^k \cdot n^2) time using a dynamic programming approach. Our algorithm is the first FPT algorithm for the Bipartite Vertex Splitting problem and has several applications in computer science and operations research.

We present HyperDegrade, a novel approach to reducing CPU power consumption by dynamically adjusting the CPU frequency. Unlike traditional approaches that rely on fixed frequency scaling, HyperDegrade uses a machine learning-based model to predict the optimal frequency for a given workload. By leveraging the observation that most workloads exhibit a significant decrease in frequency demand as they approach completion, HyperDegrade can reduce the CPU frequency to a lower value, resulting in significant power savings. Our evaluation shows that HyperDegrade can achieve an average power reduction of 23.4% and 17.1% compared to traditional frequency scaling and a state-of-the-art approach, respectively, while maintaining a negligible impact on performance.

We introduce a new unknotting operation, called the "twist-merge" operation, which is a generalization of the twist operation. This operation is applicable to both classical and welded links. We show that the twist-merge operation is a Reidemeister move, and we use this fact to prove that it is a Reidemeister move for welded links. We also show that the twist-merge operation is a generalization of the twist operation, and we use this fact to prove that it is a Reidemeister move for classical links. We then use the twist-merge operation to prove that the unknotting number of a link is equal to the minimum number of twist-merge operations required to unknot the link. We also use the twist-merge operation to prove that the welded unknotting number of a link is equal to the minimum number of twist-merge operations required to unknot the link.

This paper addresses the problem of coordinating multiple robots to accomplish a set of tasks in a network environment with limited communication and computation capabilities. The authors propose a distributed algorithm that allows robots to learn and adapt to new tasks and environments while minimizing communication overhead. The algorithm is based on a multi-task learning framework that enables robots to share knowledge and coordinate their actions in real-time. The authors demonstrate the effectiveness of their approach through simulations and experiments with a team of robots performing various tasks, including object manipulation and navigation. The results show that the proposed algorithm can achieve high task completion rates and adapt to changing environments with minimal communication overhead.

We introduce a new approach to embed a group G into a wreath product of a group H with a direct product of groups, which we call the Cartesian decomposition approach. This approach is based on the idea of decomposing the group G into a direct product of subgroups, each of which is isomorphic to a subgroup of H. We show that this approach can be used to embed G into a wreath product of H with a direct product of groups, and we provide a general formula for the wreath product. We also show that this approach can be used to embed G into a wreath product of H with a direct product of groups, where the direct product is a direct product of groups of the same order. We provide several examples to illustrate the power of this approach, including the embedding of the symmetric group S_n into a wreath product of the cyclic group of order n with a direct product of groups.

This paper explores the non-overlapping visibility regions in XL-MIMO random access protocol. The XL-MIMO random access protocol is a novel approach that enables multiple users to access the network simultaneously, improving the overall system capacity. The non-overlapping visibility regions are a critical aspect of this protocol, as they determine the number of users that can be supported in a given area. The authors of this paper propose a novel algorithm to determine the non-overlapping visibility regions, which takes into account the channel state information and the user locations. The algorithm is shown to be efficient and effective, and it is able to support a large number of users in a given area. The results of this paper demonstrate the potential of the XL-MIMO random access protocol to improve the capacity of wireless networks.

We propose a novel neural text generation model that incorporates an $n$-gram language model as a residual component. This approach leverages the strengths of both neural and traditional language models, allowing the model to learn from the patterns and structures of the $n$-gram model while still benefiting from the flexibility and expressiveness of the neural network. Our experiments demonstrate that the proposed model outperforms state-of-the-art neural text generation models in terms of both quality and efficiency, making it a promising approach for a wide range of natural language processing tasks.

We present iOCR, a novel informed optical character recognition (OCR) system designed to accurately extract election ballot tallies from scanned images. Our approach leverages a combination of machine learning and computer vision techniques to address the challenges of OCR in this domain. We develop a custom dataset of 1,000 images of scanned ballots, which we use to train a deep learning model that learns to recognize the unique patterns and layouts of election ballots. We also develop a set of rules-based heuristics to handle cases where the OCR model is uncertain or fails to recognize a tally. Our evaluation shows that iOCR achieves a high accuracy of 95.6% in extracting ballot tallies, outperforming state-of-the-art OCR systems. We also demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in a real-world election scenario, where we use iOCR to extract tallies from a set of scanned ballots and compare them to the official results. Our results show that iOCR is a reliable and accurate tool for extracting election ballot tallies from scanned images, and we believe that it has the potential to improve the efficiency and accuracy of election auditing and verification processes.

The paper titled "Comparative terrestrial atmospheric circulation regimes in simplified global circulation models: I. from cyclostrophic super-rotation to geostrophic turbulence" explores the atmospheric circulation regimes in simplified global circulation models. The authors investigate the transition from cyclostrophic super-rotation to geostrophic turbulence in these models. They find that the transition is characterized by a change in the dominant balance between the Coriolis force and the pressure gradient force. The authors also identify a critical value of the Rossby number, below which the flow becomes turbulent. The study provides insights into the dynamics of atmospheric circulation and the role of the Coriolis force in shaping the flow.

We derive a family of regularized integral representations of the reciprocal Gamma function, which are valid for all complex numbers except non-positive integers. These representations are obtained by applying the Hankel contour integral representation of the reciprocal Gamma function to a family of entire functions that are related to the reciprocal Gamma function. We then use these representations to derive a family of regularized integral representations of the reciprocal Gamma function, which are valid for all complex numbers except non-positive integers. These representations are expressed in terms of the Hankel contour integral representation of the reciprocal Gamma function and a family of entire functions that are related to the reciprocal Gamma function. We also derive a family of regularized integral representations of the reciprocal Gamma function in terms of the Hankel contour integral representation of the reciprocal Gamma function and a family of entire functions that are related to the reciprocal Gamma function. These representations are valid for all complex numbers except non-positive integers.

We develop a phase-space stochastic quantum hydrodynamics (PSQHD) approach for interacting Bose gases, which combines the strengths of stochastic methods and quantum hydrodynamics. Our approach is based on a stochastic Liouville equation for the one-body reduced density matrix, which is then used to derive a set of stochastic hydrodynamic equations for the local density and velocity fields. We show that the PSQHD equations can be mapped onto a set of stochastic Gross-Pitaevskii equations, which describe the time evolution of the local density and velocity fields. We also derive a set of stochastic equations for the local energy and momentum densities, which are essential for understanding the dynamics of interacting Bose gases. Our approach provides a new framework for studying the dynamics of interacting Bose gases, and we demonstrate its applicability by solving the PSQHD equations for a variety of initial conditions and system sizes.

This paper presents a comprehensive survey of the teacher-student architecture for knowledge learning, which has garnered significant attention in recent years due to its potential to improve the efficiency and effectiveness of knowledge learning. The teacher-student architecture is a type of meta-learning framework that enables a teacher model to learn how to teach a student model, allowing the student model to learn from the teacher model and improve its performance over time. The paper provides an overview of the key components of the teacher-student architecture, including the teacher model, student model, and knowledge graph, as well as the various techniques used to implement these components. The paper also discusses the applications of the teacher-student architecture in various domains, including natural language processing, computer vision, and reinforcement learning. Additionally, the paper presents a comprehensive evaluation of the existing literature on the teacher-student architecture, highlighting its strengths and limitations, and providing insights into future research directions.

We introduce a novel function representation, called the "factorised function representation" (FFR), which is a compact and efficient way to represent functions in graphical models. The FFR is based on a factorisation of the function into a product of smaller functions, each of which is associated with a subset of the variables. This representation allows for faster exact computation of the marginal polytope (MPE) and constrained optimisation in graphical models. We demonstrate the effectiveness of the FFR through experiments on a range of benchmark problems, showing that it can lead to significant speedups over existing methods.

We study the Racah algebra, which is the centralizer of the $n$-th power of the standard Cartan subalgebra in the enveloping algebra of the Lie algebra $\mathfrak{sl}_2$. We show that the Racah algebra is isomorphic to the algebra of polynomials in $n$ variables with the action of the symmetric group $S_n$ given by the permuting the variables. We also show that the Racah algebra is isomorphic to the algebra of polynomials in $n$ variables with the action of the symmetric group $S_n$ given by the permuting the variables. We then compute the Hilbert-Poincaré series of the Racah algebra, which is the generating function for the dimensions of the graded components of the algebra. We propose a new method for paired-permutation testing that is exact and can handle structured test statistics. The method is based on the idea of using the permutation distribution of the test statistic under the null hypothesis to compute the p-value. We show that the permutation distribution can be approximated using a normal distribution, which allows us to compute the p-value exactly. We also show that the method can handle structured test statistics, such as those that are based on the sum or product of multiple variables. We demonstrate the effectiveness of the method using a simulation study and a real-world example.

We investigate the triangular flow $v_3$ in Au+Au and Cu+Cu collisions using a multiphase transport model. The model is able to reproduce the experimental data for $v_3$ in Au+Au collisions at $\sqrt{s_{NN}}=200$ GeV, and the results are consistent with the expectations from the hydrodynamic model. However, the model fails to reproduce the experimental data for $v_3$ in Cu+Cu collisions at $\sqrt{s_{NN}}=200$ GeV. We find that the discrepancy between the model results and the experimental data for $v_3$ in Cu+Cu collisions is due to the difference in the initial conditions between the model and the experiment. The model assumes a uniform initial density, while the experiment measures a non-uniform initial density. We also find that the model results for $v_3$ in Au+Cu collisions are consistent with the expectations from the hydrodynamic model.

This paper presents a novel approach to the Probability Hypothesis Density (PHD) filter, specifically the Partitioned Multi-Bernoulli Mixture (PMBM) filter, by incorporating a partially grid-based birth model. The proposed method aims to improve the accuracy and efficiency of the PMBM filter in tracking multiple targets in cluttered environments. The partially grid-based birth model is designed to balance the trade-off between the computational complexity and the accuracy of the filter. The proposed approach is evaluated using various scenarios, including a sensor management application, where the PMBM filter is used to manage the deployment of sensors in a surveillance system. The results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method in improving the accuracy and efficiency of the PMBM filter, as well as its potential applications in sensor management.

In this paper, we propose a novel approach to optimize actions in critical situations of soccer games using deep reinforcement learning. Our method, called Deep Soccer Action Optimizer (DSAO), leverages a combination of deep neural networks and reinforcement learning to learn optimal actions in high-pressure situations. We design a custom environment for soccer games, where the agent must make decisions in real-time to achieve a goal. Our approach is based on a policy gradient method, which allows the agent to learn from trial and error. We evaluate DSAO on a set of challenging scenarios, including situations where the ball is in the opponent's penalty area, and the agent must decide whether to shoot or pass the ball. Our results show that DSAO outperforms a baseline model in terms of goal-scoring rate and decision-making speed. We also conduct an ablation study to analyze the impact of different components of our approach on the agent's performance. Our findings suggest that DSAO can be a valuable tool for optimizing actions in critical situations of soccer games, and can potentially be used in real-world applications such as sports analytics and coaching.

This paper presents a remote operation system for a single-point laser Doppler velocimeter (LDV) system to acquire 2D measurements. The system is designed to measure the velocity of particles in a fluid flow, and the remote operation system allows for the acquisition of 2D measurements by moving the LDV system in a predetermined pattern. The system consists of a computer, a motorized stage, and a single-point LDV system. The computer controls the motorized stage to move the LDV system in a predetermined pattern, and the LDV system measures the velocity of particles at each point. The data is then processed to create a 2D map of the velocity field. The system is tested in a wind tunnel and a water tunnel, and the results show that the system can accurately measure the velocity of particles in a fluid flow. The remote operation system allows for the acquisition of 2D measurements without the need for manual intervention, making it a useful tool for researchers and engineers.

We consider the Klein--Gordon equation coupled to an anharmonic oscillator, a model that describes the interaction between a scalar field and a harmonic oscillator. We prove the orbital stability of the ground state for the Klein--Gordon equation coupled to an anharmonic oscillator, and we also prove the spectral stability of the ground state for the Klein--Gordon equation coupled to an anharmonic oscillator.

We present a search for axion-like particles (ALPs) in the process $B^+\to K^+\gamma\gamma$ using a data sample of $122.6\,\mathrm{fb}^{-1}$ collected by the Belle II experiment. We find no evidence for ALP production and set upper limits on the ALP coupling to photons.

This paper explores the application of contextualized language models to the task of semantic change detection. The authors examine the performance of these models on a dataset of words with known semantic changes and compare it to the performance of traditional word embeddings. They find that contextualized models are better at capturing subtle semantic changes, but also highlight the challenges of using these models for this task, including the need for careful evaluation metrics and the potential for overfitting. The authors also discuss the implications of their findings for the study of semantic change and the development of more effective methods for detecting it.

We propose a novel method to constrain the properties of ultralight bosons using the spins of heavy quasars. Our approach is based on the superradiance mechanism, which can extract angular momentum from rotating black holes. We show that the superradiance process can imprint a characteristic signature on the spin distribution of heavy quasars, allowing us to constrain the mass and coupling constant of ultralight bosons. We apply our method to a sample of 14 heavy quasars with measured spins and find that the data are consistent with the superradiance mechanism. Our results provide a new window into the properties of ultralight bosons and have implications for our understanding of the interplay between black holes and the surrounding environment.

We present a path integral approach to the driven quantum harmonic oscillator using Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) methods. The path integral formulation of quantum mechanics is a powerful tool for studying quantum systems, but it can be challenging to evaluate the path integral due to the presence of non-trivial boundary conditions. We use the MCMC method to sample the path integral and obtain the quantum expectation values of the system. We demonstrate the accuracy and efficiency of our approach by comparing our results with exact analytical solutions and other numerical methods. Our results show that the MCMC method can be used to study the driven quantum harmonic oscillator with high accuracy and efficiency, even for large system sizes. We also discuss the potential applications of our approach to other quantum systems and the limitations of the method.

We present a novel approach to quantum relational Hoare logic, which we call quantum relational Hoare logic with expectations. This approach is based on the idea of using expectations to reason about the behavior of quantum systems. We define a new type of expectation, called a quantum expectation, which is a mathematical object that captures the expected behavior of a quantum system. We then use these expectations to define a new type of Hoare triple, called a quantum relational Hoare triple, which is a mathematical object that captures the expected behavior of a quantum system in relation to a classical system. We show that our quantum relational Hoare logic with expectations is sound and complete, and we provide a number of examples to illustrate its use. We also show that our approach can be used to reason about the behavior of quantum systems in a way that is more intuitive and easier to understand than traditional approaches.

We present a comprehensive analysis of the sources of bias in inferred measurements of the solar vector magnetic field (VMF) and propose a novel approach to mitigate these biases. Our analysis reveals that the commonly used method of inferring VMF from magnetograms is prone to systematic errors due to the presence of noise, the limited spatial resolution of the data, and the inherent assumptions made in the inversion process. We demonstrate that these biases can lead to significant errors in the inferred VMF, particularly in the magnetic field strength and inclination. To address these issues, we develop a new method that combines machine learning techniques with physical modeling to improve the accuracy of VMF inference. Our approach involves training a neural network to learn the relationships between the observed magnetogram data and the true VMF, while also incorporating physical constraints to ensure that the inferred VMF is physically plausible. We evaluate the performance of our method using a large dataset of synthetic magnetograms and demonstrate that it can significantly reduce the biases in the inferred VMF, particularly in the magnetic field strength and inclination. Our results have important implications for the analysis of solar magnetic field data and highlight the need for more accurate and robust methods for inferring VMF from magnetograms.

We introduce the Boolean complex of an involution, a combinatorial object that encodes the structure of the involution's fixed points and cycles. We show that the Boolean complex is a shellable complex, and we use this property to compute its homology groups. We also study the Boolean complex of a product of involutions, and we show that it is isomorphic to the product of the Boolean complexes of the individual involutions. We apply our results to the study of the homology of the space of involutions on a finite set, and we show that it is isomorphic to the homology of the Boolean complex of the involution.

In this paper, we investigate timelike Bertrand curves in semi-Euclidean space. We first recall the definition of Bertrand curves and their properties. Then, we introduce the concept of timelike Bertrand curves in semi-Euclidean space and derive their differential equations. We also discuss the relationship between timelike Bertrand curves and their associated curves. Furthermore, we investigate the properties of timelike Bertrand curves, such as their geodesic curvature and their relation to the curvature of the ambient space. Finally, we provide examples of timelike Bertrand curves in semi-Euclidean space and discuss their geometric and physical implications.

This paper explores the impact of loss function variation on deep learning models for classification tasks. The authors examine the effects of different loss functions on model performance, focusing on the trade-off between accuracy and robustness. They propose a novel approach to loss function selection, using a combination of cross-validation and robustness metrics to identify the optimal loss function for a given dataset. The results show that the choice of loss function can significantly impact model performance, with some loss functions leading to improved accuracy and others resulting in increased robustness. The authors also investigate the relationship between loss function and model architecture, finding that certain loss functions are more suitable for specific architectures. The findings of this study have implications for the development of deep learning models, highlighting the importance of carefully selecting the loss function to achieve optimal performance.

We present ATOMIC, a comprehensive atlas of machine commonsense for if-then reasoning. Our work focuses on the development of a large-scale, high-quality dataset that captures a wide range of everyday situations and their corresponding consequences. We introduce a novel framework for annotating and evaluating if-then reasoning, which enables us to assess the performance of models on a broad spectrum of tasks. Our dataset comprises over 300,000 if-then pairs, covering various domains and scenarios, and is designed to facilitate the development of more robust and generalizable AI systems. We demonstrate the effectiveness of ATOMIC in evaluating the performance of state-of-the-art models and provide insights into the challenges and limitations of if-then reasoning. Our work has significant implications for the development of more advanced AI systems that can reason and make decisions in complex, real-world scenarios.

We propose a novel video prediction model that leverages a dual representation to capture both the spatial and temporal dependencies in videos. Our model, called Dual Representation Video Predictor (DRVP), consists of two separate encoders that process the input video frames in parallel. The first encoder, called the spatial encoder, focuses on capturing the spatial dependencies between pixels in each frame, while the second encoder, called the temporal encoder, focuses on capturing the temporal dependencies between consecutive frames. The outputs of the two encoders are then combined using a fusion module to generate a single representation that captures both spatial and temporal dependencies. This representation is then fed into a decoder to predict the future frames of the video. We evaluate our model on several benchmark datasets and show that it outperforms state-of-the-art video prediction models in terms of both quantitative and qualitative metrics.

We introduce the truncated metric dimension of a graph, which is a variation of the metric dimension that takes into account the distances between vertices. We show that the truncated metric dimension is NP-hard to compute and provide a polynomial-time algorithm for computing it in the case of trees. We also show that the truncated metric dimension is at least as large as the metric dimension and at most as large as the vertex cover number. We provide a number of examples to illustrate the differences between the truncated metric dimension and the metric dimension.

This paper presents a novel approach to heart sound classification that considers the effects of additive noise and convolutional distortion. The proposed method utilizes a convolutional neural network (CNN) to extract features from heart sound signals, which are then used to classify the sounds into different categories. The CNN is trained on a dataset of heart sound signals that have been corrupted with additive noise and convolutional distortion, allowing it to learn robust features that are invariant to these types of noise. The proposed method is evaluated on a dataset of heart sound signals that have been corrupted with additive noise and convolutional distortion, and is shown to outperform existing methods in terms of classification accuracy. The results of this study demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method in classifying heart sounds in the presence of noise and distortion, and highlight the importance of considering these factors in the development of heart sound classification systems.

The subthermal excitation of the C{\sc i} lines in the molecular gas reservoirs of galaxies is a phenomenon that has garnered significant attention in recent years. This phenomenon is characterized by the excitation of the C{\sc i} lines to levels above the ground state, but below the thermal equilibrium level. The subthermal excitation of the C{\sc i} lines is significant because it can provide valuable insights into the physical conditions of the molecular gas reservoirs in galaxies. The subthermal excitation of the C{\sc i} lines can be used to infer the density, temperature, and metallicity of the molecular gas, as well as the presence of magnetic fields and turbulence. Furthermore, the subthermal excitation of the C{\sc i} lines can be used to study the chemical evolution of galaxies and the formation of stars. The subthermal excitation of the C{\sc i} lines is a potential utility for understanding the physical conditions of the molecular gas reservoirs in galaxies, and for studying the chemical evolution of galaxies and the formation of stars.

We introduce the ASEP speed process, a continuous-time Markov process that generalizes the asymmetric simple exclusion process (ASEP) to the setting of continuous time. The ASEP speed process is a continuous-time Markov process on the one-dimensional integer lattice, where particles jump to the right with rate 1 and to the left with rate 1 + \lambda \theta(x - y), where \theta is the Heaviside step function and \lambda is a parameter. We show that the ASEP speed process is a continuous-time Markov process with a finite state space, and we derive its generator. We also show that the ASEP speed process is a continuous-time Markov process with a finite state space, and we derive its generator. We then use the ASEP speed process to model the motion of particles in a one-dimensional lattice, and we show that the process converges to a stationary distribution as time goes to infinity. We also show that the ASEP speed process is a continuous-time Markov process with a finite state space, and we derive its generator. We then use the ASEP speed process to model the motion of particles in a one-dimensional lattice, and we show that the process converges to a stationary distribution as time goes to infinity.

The COVID-19 pandemic has highlighted the importance of mathematical models in understanding and predicting the spread of infectious diseases. This paper provides a comprehensive overview of the current state of mathematical modelling in epidemiology, with a focus on the SARS-CoV-2 epidemic. We discuss the key features of mathematical models, including compartmental models, network models, and individual-based models, and their applications in understanding the dynamics of infectious disease spread. We also examine the role of data in model development and the challenges of model calibration and validation. Furthermore, we discuss the limitations of mathematical models and the need for a more nuanced understanding of the complex interactions between humans, animals, and the environment that drive the spread of infectious diseases. Finally, we highlight the potential of mathematical models to inform public health policy and decision-making, and to support the development of effective interventions to control and prevent the spread of infectious diseases.

The M*-SFR relation, which describes the relationship between the stellar mass of galaxies and their star formation rates, has been observed to turn over at high masses. This turnover is thought to be driven by the presence of bulges in massive galaxies. Bulges are the central, older regions of galaxies that are thought to be the result of mergers and the growth of supermassive black holes. In this paper, we investigate the role of bulges in driving the M*-SFR relation turnover. We use a sample of galaxies from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey and the Galaxy Evolution Explorer to examine the relationship between bulge mass and star formation rate. We find that the presence of a bulge is a key driver of the M*-SFR relation turnover, with bulge-dominated galaxies exhibiting lower star formation rates than disk-dominated galaxies of similar mass. We also find that the bulge mass is a more important predictor of star formation rate than the total stellar mass of the galaxy. Our results suggest that the growth of bulges through mergers and the accretion of gas is a key process in shaping the M*-SFR relation and driving the turnover at high masses.

This paper presents a novel multi-task learning approach for cross-lingual sentiment analysis, which leverages the shared knowledge between sentiment analysis and language modeling tasks to improve the performance of sentiment analysis in low-resource languages. The proposed approach, called Cross-Lingual Sentiment Analysis (CLSA), consists of two main components: a language model and a sentiment analysis model. The language model is trained on a large corpus of text data in multiple languages, while the sentiment analysis model is trained on a smaller corpus of labeled sentiment data. The two models are connected through a shared embedding space, where the language model's output is used as input to the sentiment analysis model. The CLSA approach is evaluated on several benchmark datasets in multiple languages, including English, Spanish, French, German, Chinese, and Arabic. The results show that the proposed approach outperforms state-of-the-art methods in cross-lingual sentiment analysis, achieving an average improvement of 10.3% in accuracy. The CLSA approach also demonstrates its ability to adapt to new languages with limited training data, achieving an average improvement of 15.6% in accuracy when trained on a small corpus of labeled data.

We present a comprehensive analysis of the Kepler space telescope data for the star KIC 9246715, which exhibits a significant decrease in brightness over a period of 1.5 years. Our analysis reveals that the star's surface temperature has increased by 100 K, and its radius has expanded by 10%. We propose two possible explanations for this phenomenon: planetary engulfment or unexpected angular momentum transport.

This paper proposes a novel approach to detecting fake news by leveraging multimodal information and meta learning. The proposed method, called Meta Neural Process Networks (MNP), combines the strengths of neural process networks and meta learning to effectively capture the underlying patterns in fake news detection. MNP is trained on a dataset of real and fake news articles, which are represented as multimodal inputs consisting of text, images, and audio. The model learns to adapt to new, unseen data by leveraging the knowledge gained from the training process. The results show that MNP outperforms state-of-the-art methods in detecting fake news, demonstrating its potential as a robust and effective approach for this task.

We present a new method for constructing polyphase Golay complementary arrays (PGCAs) using a combination of the polyphase Golay complementary sequences (PGCSs) and the polyphase Golay complementary arrays (PGCAs) with a specific structure. The proposed method is based on the fact that the polyphase Golay complementary sequences can be used to construct the polyphase Golay complementary arrays with a specific structure. We show that the proposed method can be used to construct PGCAs with a large number of elements and a high degree of symmetry. We also show that the proposed method can be used to construct PGCAs with a specific structure, such as the PGCAs with a rectangular lattice. The proposed method is compared with the existing methods for constructing PGCAs, and it is shown that the proposed method has several advantages over the existing methods.

This paper presents a novel approach to synthesizing brain lesions using a progressive adversarial variational autoencoder (PAVAE). The proposed method leverages a hierarchical structure to progressively refine the lesion synthesis process, allowing for the generation of realistic and diverse brain lesions. The PAVAE model consists of multiple stages, each responsible for generating a specific aspect of the lesion, such as shape, size, and location. The model is trained using a combination of adversarial and variational objectives, which enables it to learn a probabilistic representation of the lesion data. The proposed method is evaluated on a large dataset of brain lesions, demonstrating its ability to generate realistic and diverse lesions that are comparable to real-world data. The results show that the PAVAE model outperforms existing methods in terms of lesion synthesis quality and diversity.

This paper presents a unified framework for feature extraction based on contrastive learning. The proposed framework, called Unified Contrastive Learning (UCL), integrates multiple contrastive learning methods into a single framework, allowing for the extraction of robust and transferable features. UCL is based on the idea of learning a common representation space for different tasks and datasets, which enables the transfer of knowledge across tasks and domains. The framework consists of three main components: a feature extractor, a contrastive loss function, and a projection head. The feature extractor is responsible for extracting features from the input data, the contrastive loss function is used to learn a common representation space, and the projection head is used to project the features into a lower-dimensional space. UCL is evaluated on several benchmark datasets, including ImageNet, CIFAR-10, and STL-10, and is shown to outperform state-of-the-art methods in terms of feature quality and transferability. The results demonstrate the effectiveness of UCL in extracting robust and transferable features, and its potential applications in various computer vision tasks.

We present SKILL, a novel approach to infusing structured knowledge into large language models. SKILL leverages a combination of knowledge graph embeddings and a novel knowledge graph attention mechanism to effectively incorporate structured knowledge into the model. We demonstrate the effectiveness of SKILL on a range of knowledge-intensive tasks, including question answering, entity recognition, and text classification. Our results show that SKILL outperforms state-of-the-art models on these tasks, and that the knowledge graph attention mechanism is a key component of its success. We also provide an analysis of the knowledge graph attention mechanism and its role in SKILL's performance.

We investigate the shadow thermodynamics of non-linear charged Anti-de Sitter black holes. The shadow is a dark region in the vicinity of a black hole, which is formed by the bending of light around it. We consider a non-linear charged Anti-de Sitter black hole, which is a solution to the Einstein-Maxwell-dilaton gravity theory. We calculate the shadow radius and the shadow area of this black hole, and we find that they are both functions of the black hole's mass, charge, and dilaton coupling constant. We also calculate the temperature and entropy of the black hole, and we find that they are both functions of the black hole's mass, charge, and dilaton coupling constant. We then use the first law of black hole thermodynamics to relate the shadow radius and the shadow area to the temperature and entropy of the black hole. We find that the shadow radius and the shadow area are both proportional to the temperature and entropy of the black hole, and we obtain a universal relation between the shadow radius and the shadow area. Our results provide a new understanding of the thermodynamics of non-linear charged Anti-de Sitter black holes, and they have implications for the study of black hole physics and cosmology.

We investigate the entanglement and synchronization properties of a two-qubit system in the presence of a time-dependent interaction. We find that the entanglement and synchronization properties exhibit distinct manifestations of the changes in the interaction strength. Specifically, we observe that the entanglement exhibits a sudden death and revival phenomenon, while the synchronization exhibits a sudden onset and disappearance phenomenon. We also find that the tomograms of the system exhibit distinct features that reflect the changes in the entanglement and synchronization properties. Our results provide new insights into the behavior of entangled systems and the role of synchronization in quantum information processing.

We present the first observation of the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0 K^0_S$ decay and evidence for the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^{*0} K^0_S$ decay, using a sample of $pp$ collisions at $\sqrt{s}=13$ TeV collected by the LHCb experiment. The $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0 K^0_S$ decay is observed with a significance of $5.1\sigma$, while the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^{*0} K^0_S$ decay is observed with a significance of $3.4\sigma$. The branching fractions are measured to be $\mathcal{B}(B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0 K^0_S)=(1.15\pm0.23\pm0.07)\times10^{-4}$ and $\mathcal{B}(B^0_s\to\bar{D}^{*0} K^0_S)=(1.35\pm0.35\pm0.09)\times10^{-4}$. The results are consistent with the predictions of the factorization approach.

We consider the problem of constructing the lattice of submodules of a multiplicity-free module from partial information. Given a multiplicity-free module $M$ and a subset of submodules $S$ of $M$, we provide an algorithm to construct the lattice of submodules of $M$ that contain all submodules in $S$. Our algorithm is based on the concept of a "partial lattice" and uses a combination of combinatorial and algebraic techniques to compute the lattice. We also provide a complexity analysis of the algorithm and discuss its applications in representation theory and algebraic combinatorics.

In this paper, we investigate Biharmonic hypersurfaces in the Euclidean space. Biharmonic hypersurfaces are a generalization of harmonic hypersurfaces, and they have been studied extensively in the context of differential geometry. We consider the recurrent operators, which are a type of differential operator that is used to study the properties of hypersurfaces. Our main goal is to find the conditions under which a Biharmonic hypersurface is recurrent. We use the properties of the recurrent operators and the Biharmonic equation to derive a set of conditions that must be satisfied by the hypersurface. We then use these conditions to classify the Biharmonic hypersurfaces into different types, based on their properties. Our results provide new insights into the properties of Biharmonic hypersurfaces and have implications for the study of differential geometry.

We introduce the concept of p/q-recognisable sets, which generalise the notion of p-recognisable sets. A set is p/q-recognisable if it is the image of a p-recognisable set under a p/q-recognisable function. We show that the class of p/q-recognisable sets is closed under various operations, including union, intersection, and complementation. We also establish a connection between p/q-recognisable sets and the theory of p/q-recognisable functions.

Crackling noise is a ubiquitous phenomenon observed in various natural and artificial systems, including the peeling of adhesive tapes. Despite its widespread occurrence, the underlying mechanisms governing crackling noise remain poorly understood. Recent studies have revealed that crackling noise can be characterized by a power-law distribution of event sizes, suggesting a self-organized critical state. However, the origin of this critical state and the associated power-law behavior remains unclear. In this study, we investigate the peeling of an adhesive tape and uncover a hidden order underlying the crackling noise. Using high-speed imaging and acoustic measurements, we observe that the peeling process is accompanied by a series of discrete events, each corresponding to the detachment of a single layer of adhesive. We find that the distribution of event sizes follows a power-law, with an exponent that is consistent with the critical state observed in other systems. However, we also discover that the power-law behavior is accompanied by a hidden order, characterized by a periodic modulation of the event sizes. This modulation is found to be correlated with the underlying structure of the adhesive tape, suggesting that the critical state is not a random process, but rather a self-organized state that emerges from the interactions between the tape and the substrate. Our findings provide new insights into the mechanisms governing crackling noise and have implications for our understanding of self-organized criticality in complex systems.
